text: Lesson 24 ended on a problem: millions of individual samples stored as individual objects turn every read into its own request, and that latency adds up fast across five hundred twelve GPUs. The fix is to never store samples individually in the first place — instead, Solara-70B's corpus is packed into shards before training ever starts.

A shard is a single file, commonly a tar archive, holding hundreds or thousands of samples packed back to back. WebDataset is the library Solara AI uses to stream those tar shards straight into a PyTorch pipeline without ever extracting them. The brace expansion here names one thousand twenty four shards as a single dataset, and each DataLoader worker streams sequentially through whichever shards it's assigned — one request per shard, not one request per sample.

Shard count is a balancing act. Too few, oversized shards, and some of the five hundred twelve GPUs end up starved waiting for a worker to finish its current shard with no next one ready. Too many, undersized shards, and the per-request overhead from Lesson 24 creeps right back in. With sixty-four nodes and eight workers per node, that's five hundred twelve concurrent readers, so the rule of thumb is simple: shards should significantly outnumber the total worker count.

True random access across a multi-terabyte corpus doesn't work well against streaming object storage, so WebDataset shuffles at two levels instead. Shard-level shuffling randomizes which shard a worker reads next, and an in-memory shuffle buffer randomizes sample order within a sliding window as the shard streams past. Together they're good enough randomness without needing random-access reads, and because both are seeded, the shuffle is reproducible on resume.

Sharding trades random access for sequential, streamable reads, sized against the cluster's worker count. Next, Lesson 26: the storage backends those shards actually live on — object, block, and parallel filesystems.
